## What it generates

Generates SDKs (TypeScript, Go, Rust, Python, C#, Java), a Go command-line client and a Model Context Protocol
server from an OpenAPI 3.x document, or straight from a
[`@workerstack/backend`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@workerstack/backend) app.

Every target reads one intermediate representation and vendors its own small runtime, so a generated SDK has no
dependency on backend, and a spec from another framework generates just as well. The output is formatted and
deterministic: regenerating an unchanged spec changes nothing on disk.

## Install

backend moved to the workerstack org in 1.0.0-rc.23, and [the migration note](https://github.com/workerstack/backend/blob/main/docs/migrating-from-honey.md)
maps each old package name to its new one. 1.0 is out as a release candidate, published under npm's `next` tag, so
an install without a tag gets a deprecated placeholder.
Add `@next` until the final release:

```sh
npm install --save-dev @workerstack/clients@next
```

Node 22.12 or later, or Bun 1.3 or later.

Each target formats what it writes with that language's own formatter, when it can find it:

| target      | formatter | found by                                                                    |
| ----------- | --------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `go`, `cli` | gofmt     | `$GOFMT`, `$GOROOT/bin/gofmt`, `gofmt` on `PATH`, beside the `go` on `PATH` |
| `python`    | ruff      | `$RUFF`, then `ruff` on `PATH`                                              |
| `rust`      | rustfmt   | `$RUSTFMT`, the active toolchain's own binary beside `rustc`, `PATH`        |
| `ts`        | oxfmt     | the `oxfmt` optional peer, installed beside clients                         |

A formatter it cannot find is named on standard error and skipped: the files go out as the emitter wrote them,
which is valid source either way, so generating a Python SDK never requires you to install ruff. Set
`CLIENTS_REQUIRE_FORMATTERS=1` to make a missing formatter fail the run instead, for a pipeline that would
rather stop than ship unformatted code. An override that points at nothing is refused by name.

oxfmt is the exception and says nothing when absent: it is clients' own choice of TypeScript formatter and a
declared optional peer, so not having it is the documented normal rather than news. `CLIENTS_REQUIRE_FORMATTERS`
still stops for it.

The `csharp` and `java` targets are not formatted today: `dotnet format` and google-java-format work over a
project rather than a stream, which clients' post-pass does not yet do.

## Start

From a document:

```sh
npx clients generate --spec openapi.json --target ts --target python --out generated
```

From a backend app module, with no document written first:

```sh
npx clients generate --app src/app.ts --target ts --target go --go-module-path github.com/acme/shop/sdk \
  --out generated
```

The targets are `ts`, `go`, `rust`, `python`, `csharp`, `java`, `cli` and `mcp`. Each target's files go under
`<out>/<target>`.

## clients generate

```sh
clients generate --spec openapi.json --target ts --target cli --out generated \
  --cli-binary-name shop --cli-module-path github.com/acme/shop --cli-repo acme/shop
```

- `--spec <file>`: the OpenAPI document, as JSON.
- `--app <module>[#export]`: a backend app module instead of `--spec` (give one, never both). Its named export, else
  `app`, else `default`, is the app; its document is made by the app's own `@workerstack/backend/http/openapi`, resolved from
  the app as at run time, and the module's `openApi` export, if any, is that document's options (`info`,
  `securitySchemes`, `invalidate`, …, as `generateOpenApi` takes them). Started by `bun run`, the bin hands the load to
  that Bun, so a module needing Bun's loaders works; a run ends once it has written, whatever the module left open.
  The module exports the app and serves nothing: one that calls `serve()` as it loads is outside `--app`'s contract,
  since backend never serves implicitly and has no switch to stop it.
- `--target <name>`: `ts`, `go`, `rust`, `python`, `csharp`, `java`, `cli` or `mcp`; repeat it for more than one.
- `--out <dir>`: each target's files go under `<dir>/<target>`.
- `--<target>-<option>`: a target's options are its generator's, passed through as given. Each takes a value.
- `--watch`: generate again on each change of the spec (or the `--app` module), each run in a fresh process.
- `-h`, `--help`: the usage text, with every target's options.

Parsing is strict, because a typo that generates the wrong thing silently is worse than a refusal: an unknown flag, a
missing value, a stray argument, an unknown target, or an option for a target no `--target` names is a usage error.
`--k v` and `--k=v` both work, and a value is never the next flag.

The `--metadata-<field>` flags fill one package block that every target which publishes reads where its registry has
a place for the field, so a description or license is given once, not once per target. A target's own option of the
same meaning wins: `--java-description` over `--metadata-description`. Each field is checked before anything
generates: URLs must be https, the license an SPDX expression, text one line.

`--metadata-readme` and `--metadata-license-file` name files on disk, read once relative to where clients runs. Every
target writes them into its package root as `README.md` and `LICENSE`, and each manifest points at the ones it has:
pyproject's `readme` and `license-files`, Cargo's `readme` and `include`, the `.csproj`'s `PackageReadmeFile` and packed
items, and jsr.json's publish list; npm packs both on its own. The README must be a `.md` file, and both must be UTF-8
text. `--metadata-icon` ships only into the C# package, as `icon` with its own extension in lower case (`icon.png`,
`icon.jpeg`) under `PackageIcon`, since nuget.org is the one registry that shows an icon: a PNG or JPEG whose bytes are
that image, at most 1 MB.

## The six SDKs

Every SDK takes the same configuration — a base URL, the auth the spec's security scheme names, a timeout, retries,
hooks around each HTTP call, and per-call overrides — and every one answers the same way: the normal call returns
your value and throws a typed error by status, while `client.safe` answers a result instead. What follows is each
language's client in a slice of a compiled example; the
[SDK recipes](https://github.com/workerstack/clients/blob/main/docs/sdk-recipes.md) page has the whole programs.

### The TypeScript SDK

```sh
clients generate --spec openapi.json --target ts --out generated --ts-name Kitchen
```

```sdk ts
import { DecodeError, Kitchen, NotFoundError } from "./kitchen"

export function newClient(): Kitchen {
	return new Kitchen({
		baseURL: "https://api.example.com",
		headers: { authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.KITCHEN_TOKEN ?? ""}` },
		timeout: 10_000,
	})
}

export async function organization(client: Kitchen, orgId: string): Promise<string | null> {
	try {
		await client.organizations.retrieve({ params: { orgId } })
		return orgId
	} catch (error) {
		if (error instanceof NotFoundError) return null
		throw error
	}
}

export async function health(client: Kitchen): Promise<string> {
	const result = await client.safe.health.check()
	if (result.ok) return "up"
	if (result.error instanceof DecodeError) return `unreadable answer: ${result.error.message}`
	return `answered ${result.error.status}`
}
```

#### Publishing it to npm and JSR

The target writes a package around the SDK, so the output directory publishes as it is. The sources stay where a
workspace imports them; they import each other as `.js`, which every TypeScript resolution and bundler maps to the
`.ts` file. Node will not strip types under `node_modules`, so `dist/` holds each source compiled to ES module
JavaScript beside its declarations, and `package.json` exports those: the root, `./webhook` when the document has
webhook events, and `./tanstack-query` with `@tanstack/query-core` as an optional peer. A scoped `--ts-package-name`
also gets a `jsr.json` that publishes the sources themselves, its `.js` imports mapped to their `.ts` files.
`--metadata-*` fills description, keywords, homepage, bugs, license, author and repository.

```sh
clients generate --spec openapi.json --target ts --out generated --ts-name Kitchen \
  --ts-package-name @acme/kitchen --ts-version 1.4.0 --metadata-license MIT
```

#### TanStack Query, from the same document

`--ts-tanstack-query` writes one more file beside the SDK, `<stem>.tanstack-query.gen.ts`. It takes no value:

```sh
clients generate --spec openapi.json --target ts --out generated --ts-name Kitchen --ts-tanstack-query
```

Build the QueryClient first, then the SDK with the file's `invalidateQueries` hook, then the helpers. The
`QueryClient` is the one your framework's adapter exports (`@tanstack/solid-query`, `@tanstack/react-query`), or
query-core's own, as here:

```sdk ts tanstack
import { QueryClient } from "@tanstack/query-core"
import { Kitchen } from "./kitchen"
import { createQueryHelpers, invalidateQueries } from "./kitchen.tanstack-query.gen"

export const queryClient = new QueryClient()
const sdk = new Kitchen({ baseURL: "https://api.example.com", onInvalidate: [invalidateQueries(queryClient)] })
export const { query, mutation, infiniteQuery, queryKey, mutationKey } = createQueryHelpers(() => sdk)
```

The five surfaces are nested exactly as the client is, so `query.organizations.retrieve(…)` sits where
`client.organizations.retrieve(…)` does. `createQueryHelpers` takes a function that returns the client, and it calls it
on every request, so an isomorphic app can return a different client for each request.

The document decides what goes where. A `GET` is on `query`, every other method is on `mutation`, and an event
stream, a WebSocket or an `x-realtime` operation is on neither, because a stream is not a cache entry. Nothing
is keyed off a method's name.

**Call shapes.** Each factory returns only its key and its function. Spread the result into TanStack's own
options and put everything else after it, so every other option is typed by TanStack. These use query-core's
observers; `useQuery(() => ({ ... }))` in solid-query, or `useQuery({ ... })` in react-query, takes the same
object:

```sdk ts tanstack
import { InfiniteQueryObserver, MutationObserver, QueryClient, QueryObserver } from "@tanstack/query-core"
import { Kitchen } from "./kitchen"
import { createQueryHelpers, invalidateQueries } from "./kitchen.tanstack-query.gen"

const queryClient = new QueryClient()
const sdk = new Kitchen({ baseURL: "https://api.example.com", onInvalidate: [invalidateQueries(queryClient)] })
const { query, mutation, infiniteQuery, queryKey } = createQueryHelpers(() => sdk)

export function organization(orgId: string) {
	return new QueryObserver(queryClient, { ...query.organizations.retrieve({ params: { orgId } }), staleTime: 0 })
}

// the second argument is the SDK's own call options; they reach the call, not the key
export const timed = query.organizations.retrieve({ params: { orgId: "org_1" } }, { timeout: 5_000 })

export const greet = new MutationObserver(queryClient, {
	...mutation.hello.create(),
	onMutate: (input) => console.log(`greeting ${input.json.name}`),
})

export const greetings = new InfiniteQueryObserver(queryClient, {
	...infiniteQuery.hello.list((q: string | undefined) => ({ search: { q: q ?? "" } })),
	initialPageParam: undefined,
	getNextPageParam: () => undefined, // read the next page param off the last page, when your API pages
})

export const cached = queryClient.getQueryData(queryKey.hello.list({ search: { q: "Ada" } }))
```

A read takes the SDK method's request, then optionally its call options (`timeout`, `headers`, `signal`, and
the other per-call options). `mutate` takes exactly what the SDK method takes. A paged read takes a function
from the page param to the request. The adapter calls that function once with `undefined` to build the key, so
it must accept `undefined`. Annotate its parameter and TanStack infers the page param type from it. Every call
gets TanStack's abort signal merged with yours, so a cancel, or the last observer unmounting, aborts the
request.

**Keys.** A read's key is `[<SDK name>, ...the member path, the request]`. The request object goes in whole,
so `params`, `search` and anything else the SDK sends are all in it. That is what TanStack requires: every input
the `queryFn` depends on belongs in the key, so two reads of one route that differ only by `search` are two
cache entries. The call options are not in the key, since a signal and a timeout say nothing about the answer.
A read with no request keys as `[<SDK name>, ...the member path]`. `queryKey.<…>(req)` returns exactly the key
`query.<…>(req)` uses, typed so `getQueryData` infers the answer. A paged read's key is the key of its request
for `undefined` plus a trailing `"infinite"` marker, because its cached shape is `InfiniteData` and it must not
share the plain read's entry.

**Invalidation** happens in the SDK, not the helpers. A successful write fires the SDK's `onInvalidate` with the
reads its `x-invalidate` selectors name, and `invalidateQueries(queryClient)` makes each of them stale as
`[<SDK name>, ...the member path, { params }]`, or as the bare prefix when the target has no params. TanStack
matches objects partially and compares only the filter's own positions, so that reaches every search of that
read, the paged entry included. Because the SDK fires the hook, a plain `sdk.hello.create(…)` refreshes the
cache just as `mutation.hello.create()` does. The SDK awaits the hook, so a write resolves only after the
active reads it made stale have refetched. A failing refetch holds the write through its retries but never
rejects it, and an infinite query refetches every page it holds.

**Server rendering.** On the server, build the QueryClient and the SDK per request, in that order. Both are
dropped when the request ends, and the hook holds no state of its own. If a route preload prefetches, skip the
browser's hydration run, or it refetches what the server already sent:

```sdk ts tanstack
import { QueryClient } from "@tanstack/query-core"
import { Kitchen } from "./kitchen"
import { createQueryHelpers, invalidateQueries } from "./kitchen.tanstack-query.gen"

const queryClient = new QueryClient()
const sdk = new Kitchen({ baseURL: "https://api.example.com", onInvalidate: [invalidateQueries(queryClient)] })
const { query } = createQueryHelpers(() => sdk)

// a route preload: `isServer` from your framework (`@solidjs/web` in Solid), `intent` from the router
export function preloadOrganization(isServer: boolean, intent: string, orgId: string): void {
	if (!isServer && intent === "initial") return
	void queryClient.prefetchQuery(query.organizations.retrieve({ params: { orgId } }))
}
```

`@tanstack/query-core` is your dependency, not backend's. Install it yourself; the file imports it for types
only.

Drop the flag and the next run deletes the file, the way `.clients-generated.json` deletes anything the previous
run wrote and this one did not. The index file never re-exports the adapter, so an SDK generated without the
flag names no TanStack type anywhere.

#### Single-flight, a write and its reads in one request

`--ts-single-flight` writes `<stem>.single-flight.gen.ts`, a server's file: `singleFlightHandler(getSdk, options)`
is a fetch handler, and `runSingleFlight(sdk, body)` runs the same batch with no Request or Response. It takes no
value, and the run refuses it for a document with no write whose `x-invalidate` names a read.

```sh
clients generate --spec openapi.json --target ts --out generated --ts-name Kitchen --ts-single-flight
```

A batch is `{ v: 1, op, input, reads: [{ id, operationId, input }] }` and its answer is
`{ v: 1, write: { status, headers, body }, reads: [{ id, data } | { id, error: { status, body? } }] }`. Everything
is checked against the service map before anything runs: one REST write, at most `maxReads` (10) REST JSON reads,
and input of only `params`, `search`, `json` (the write's) and `idempotencyKey` (an idempotent write's). The
handler takes only a JSON POST of at most `maxBodyBytes` (64 KiB), refuses a browser on another site or an origin
outside `allowedOrigins` (its own by default), and answers a refusal as a 400 `application/problem+json`.

The write runs once on `getSdk(request)`, which you make per request, forwarding only the auth you choose; the
handler adds no retry, though the SDK's own hooks may. Only after a 2xx do the reads run, in parallel and past any
cache, within `readBudgetMs` (2000) and `maxReadBytes` (1 MiB) in all; a read past either ends as its own error
entry (504 or 502) and never fails the batch. The write's `Set-Cookie` headers are copied onto the 200, and a
cookie only sticks when the API shares the handler's site.

The index never re-exports the file, so no browser bundle carries the handler; the package exports it at
`./single-flight`.

The client sends its writes there once you give it `singleFlight`. A write goes in a batch only when it can: a
REST write with a JSON answer whose `x-invalidate` names reads, called with nothing a batch cannot carry
(`headers`, `cookies`, `body`, `form`, `baseURL`, `raw`), its operationId not in `exclude`, and `select` picking at
least one read. `select` gets the write's targets and returns the reads to bring back, at most `maxReads` (10).
Every other call goes direct, as does one called with `singleFlight: false`. The batch is a POST to `path`
(`_mutate`) under the base URL, so the client's hooks, timeout and signal apply to it. An idempotent write's key
is made before the batch, so a resend carries the same one. With TanStack Query, `activeReads(queryClient)` picks
the active reads, and `invalidateQueries` puts each one in the cache before it marks the rest stale:

```sdk ts tanstack
import { QueryClient } from "@tanstack/query-core"
import { Kitchen } from "./kitchen"
import { activeReads, invalidateQueries } from "./kitchen.tanstack-query.gen"

const queryClient = new QueryClient()
const sdk = new Kitchen({
	baseURL: "https://app.example.com/api",
	onInvalidate: [invalidateQueries(queryClient)],
	singleFlight: { select: activeReads(queryClient) },
})
```

The write resolves with the answer a direct call would have, and throws the same error. Its reads reach the
`onInvalidate` hooks first, as `event.fresh`: each answered read's data by the id `select` gave it, and in
`failed` the ids that did not come back. A query opts out with `meta: { singleFlight: false }`, and a mutation with
the same meta sends its write direct. A 401 on the write refreshes the token once through `onAuthExpired` and sends
the batch again. When the handler refuses the batch, the client sends the write direct; any other failure throws
and the write is never sent twice. A batch answer that is no envelope throws `DecodeError`, the hooks still
called, since the write may have run.

`send` replaces the POST, for an app that calls its server another way, such as a server function that returns
`runSingleFlight(sdk, batch)`. It gets the batch and resolves the envelope. The client cannot tell a refusal
through `send` from a failure, so it throws one and never resends the write:

```sdk ts
import { Kitchen, type SingleFlightBatch } from "./kitchen"

declare function mutate(batch: SingleFlightBatch): Promise<object>

export const sdk = new Kitchen({
	baseURL: "https://app.example.com/api",
	singleFlight: {
		select: (targets) =>
			targets.map((target, at) => ({ id: `r${at}`, input: { params: target.params }, operationId: target.operationId })),
		send: mutate,
	},
})
```

### The Go SDK

Idiomatic Go: a `Config`, `context.Context` on every call, errors read with `errors.As`, and an event stream as a
`range` over a function.

```sh
clients generate --spec openapi.json --target go --out generated --go-module-path github.com/acme/shop/sdk
```

Go wants a v2-or-later module's major version at the end of its path, so pass the base path and the version:
`--go-version 2.1.0` makes go.mod declare `github.com/acme/shop/sdk/v2`, and the CLI target's `--cli-version` does the
same for its module and the version it links in. A path Go would not publish (no domain first, or a suffix such as
`/v1`) is refused, as is a suffix next to a version, since the version gives it.

```go
func listing(ctx context.Context, client *sdk.Client) string {
	r, err := client.Safe().Root.List(ctx, nil)
	if err != nil {
		return fmt.Sprintf("no answer: %v", err) // never sent, refused, dropped, timed out or canceled
	}
	var unreadable *sdk.DecodeError
	var failed *sdk.ClientError
	switch {
	case r.Ok():
		return fmt.Sprintf("answered %d: %v", r.Response.StatusCode, r.Data)
	case errors.As(r.Err, &unreadable):
		return fmt.Sprintf("answered %d, unreadable: %v", r.Response.StatusCode, unreadable.Err)
	case errors.As(r.Err, &failed):
		return fmt.Sprintf("answered %d: %s", failed.StatusCode, failed.Key)
	}
	return r.Err.Error()
}
```

### The Rust SDK

Async over `reqwest`, each call taking its options struct, with the safe mirror as a second client style.

```sh
clients generate --spec openapi.json --target rust --out generated --rust-crate-name shop-sdk
```

```rust
async fn listing(client: &Client) -> String {
    match client.safe().root().list(&RootListOpts::default()).await {
        Ok(Answer::Ok { data, response }) => format!("answered {}: {data:?}", response.status),
        Ok(Answer::Err {
            error: SafeError::Api(failed),
            response,
        }) => format!("answered {}: {}", response.status, failed.message()),
        Ok(Answer::Err {
            error: SafeError::Decode(unreadable),
            response,
        }) => format!("answered {}, unreadable: {unreadable}", response.status),
        Err(no_answer) => format!("no answer: {no_answer}"), // never sent, refused, timed out or canceled
    }
}
```

### The Python SDK

A sync `SDK` and an async `AsyncSDK`, both context managers, typed for `mypy --strict`, with results as frozen
dataclasses to narrow with `match`.

```sh
clients generate --spec openapi.json --target python --out generated --python-package-name shop_sdk
```

`pyproject.toml` builds with hatchling and carries what PyPI shows: `--metadata-*` gives the description, the SPDX
`license` (PEP 639, so no `License ::` classifier), authors, keywords, and `[project.urls]` (Homepage, Source,
Issues, Documentation, Changelog). The classifiers name the Python versions clients tests and `Typing :: Typed`, and
clients' own manifest stays out of the sdist.

```python
async def health(client: AsyncSDK) -> str:
    match await client.safe.health.check():
        case Ok(data, response):
            return f"answered {response.status}: {data}"
        case Err(DecodeError() as unreadable, response):
            return f"answered {response.status}, unreadable: {unreadable}"
        case Err(error, response):
            return f"answered {response.status}: {error}"
```

### The C# SDK

A .NET project with its own `HttpClient` pipeline, `IAsyncDisposable` streams, and `client.Safe` answering
`Result<T>`.

```sh
clients generate --spec openapi.json --target csharp --out generated --csharp-package-id Acme.Shop
```

nuget.org shows a package's description, authors, license and links: give them with `--csharp-description`,
`--csharp-authors`, `--csharp-license`, `--csharp-homepage` and `--csharp-repository`, and the `.csproj` carries them
into `dotnet pack`.

```csharp
    public static async Task<string> Listing(HttpSdkClient client, string id)
    {
        var result = await client.Safe.Root.ListAsync(id); // no answer (never sent, refused, timed out, canceled) still throws
        return result.Match(
            found => $"answered {result.Response.Status}: {found}",
            error => error switch
            {
                DecodeException unreadable => $"answered {result.Response.Status}, unreadable: {unreadable.Message}",
                ApiStatusException failed => $"answered {failed.Status}: {failed.Key}",
                _ => error.Message,
            });
    }
```

### The Java SDK

A Java 17 library on Jackson 3, with builders, `try`-with-resources streams, `client.safe()` answering a sealed
`Result<T>`, and a Gradle publication.

```sh
clients generate --spec openapi.json --target java --out generated --java-group-id com.acme
```

Maven Central refuses a POM without a URL, a license, a developer and scm: give them with `--java-homepage`,
`--java-license`, `--java-developers "Name <email>, Other Name"` and `--java-repository`, or once for every target in
the metadata block, whose authors are the POM's developers. Signing the publication stays yours.

```java
  static String listing(KitchenClient client) {
    // no answer (never sent, refused, timed out, canceled) still throws
    Result<ListApiResponse200> result = client.safe().root().list(RootListParams.builder().build());
    int status = result.response().status();
    return result.fold(
        found -> "answered " + status + ": " + found,
        error ->
            error instanceof ApiException failed
                ? "answered " + status + ": " + failed.key()
                : "answered " + status + ", unreadable: " + error.getMessage());
  }
```

## Errors and the safe mirror

Two styles, in all six SDKs, over the same calls:

- **The normal call** answers its value and throws on any failure: an error status as its typed error
  (`NotFoundError` and so on, each a `ClientError`), and an undecodable or over-cap 2xx as a `DecodeError`.
- **`client.safe`** holds the same calls, each answering a result. On `ok` it carries the data, the raw response, and
  the declared response headers when the operation has any. Otherwise it carries the error the normal call would have
  thrown, with the parsed body on it. A declared status narrows the error's type and body; any other status is the
  base client error with an `unknown` body.
- **No answer throws in both styles.** A call never sent, a refused or dropped connection, a timeout, a cancel, and a
  stream that drops after it opened are not answers, so there is nothing for a result to carry.

A name of yours that collides with the mirror, or with a runtime type, is renamed and reported on stderr — never
silently. An operation or root resource named `safe` becomes `safe_`, and a component named like one of the runtime
types becomes `<Name>Model`.

Full reference: [generated clients](https://github.com/workerstack/clients/blob/main/docs/client.md).

## The command-line client

`--target cli` writes a Go command-line client for the API: one command per operation, grouped by its dotted
`operationId`, with `--help` everywhere, `commands` and `schema` for discovery, typed flags, table/JSON/NDJSON/YAML
output, streams, pagination, shell completion, and an embedded `SKILL.md` so an agent can drive it. It ships with a
release workflow, which can publish to Homebrew, Scoop, winget, AUR and deb/rpm/apk packages, and, with `--cli-repo`,
install scripts that verify what they install.

```sh
clients generate --spec openapi.json --target cli --out ./cli --cli-repo acme/shop-cli
shop orders list --status open --output json
```

| Value                                                               | Default         | What it does                                         |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| a command per operation                                             | —               | grouped by the dotted operationId resource tree      |
| `--json`                                                            | off             | one machine-readable shape on every command          |
| `--output <json\|ndjson\|yaml\|table>`                              | table           | human and machine formats                            |
| `--api-key` / `--base-url` / `--config` / `--timeout` / `--verbose` | from config/env | auth, target, config file, deadline, logging         |
| `commands`, `schema`                                                | —               | a listable command index and per-call schemas        |
| `--output <file>`                                                   | stdout          | a binary response written as bytes, pipe-safe        |
| exit codes                                                          | usage/standard  | non-zero on usage error, distinct from a runtime one |

Its configuration has one precedence, everywhere: **flag, then environment, then config file.** The environment
variables are the `--cli-env-prefix` (or the API's name) upper-cased.

Full reference: [the generated CLI](https://github.com/workerstack/clients/blob/main/docs/cli.md) and
[releasing it](https://github.com/workerstack/clients/blob/main/docs/cli-release.md).

## Install scripts

The CLI's `install.sh` and `install.ps1` are written by installgen, which ships in this package as the `installgen`
bin and the `@workerstack/clients/installers` library (it was `@lovrozagar/installgen`). The generated release
workflow checks every release with the installgen of the clients release that generated the module:

```sh
npx --yes --package @workerstack/clients@<version> installgen check --default-version v1.2.3
```

installgen also writes installers for any prebuilt binary, outside a generated CLI:

```ts
import { defineConfig } from "@workerstack/clients/installers"

export default defineConfig({
	name: "my-cli",
	baseUrl: "https://dl.example.com/my-cli",
	assetPath: ({ version, os, arch }) => `${version}/my-cli-${os}-${arch}.tar.gz`,
})
```

Full reference: [installgen](https://github.com/workerstack/clients/blob/main/src/installers/README.md).

## Release tooling

`clients release` cuts versions for a product's public packages and mirrors each one to its own GitHub repo.
A product describes its packages once, in a `release.config.ts` typed by the `@workerstack/clients/release`
library; each package's dir sits beside the config, and the repo root is the config's git toplevel:

```ts
import { defineRelease } from "@workerstack/clients/release"

export default defineRelease({
	project: "acme",
	codegen: ["bun", "run", "codegen"],
	homepage: "https://example.com",
	spec: { committedPath: "openapi.json", deployedUrl: "https://api.example.com/openapi.json" },
	packages: [
		{ name: "sdk", repo: "acme/sdk", description: "Acme SDK", commitMessage: "chore: sync", topics: ["acme"] },
	],
})
```

```sh
clients release bump --config acme-release/release.config.ts [--major]
clients release sync --config acme-release/release.config.ts [--only sdk] [--dry-run] [--validate-only]
clients release bootstrap --config acme-release/release.config.ts (--all | --only sdk) [--force-bootstrap]
```

`bump` writes each changed package's version files, `CHANGELOG.md` and `.release-state.json` (an API change is a
minor, measured by oasdiff through Go on PATH); `sync` and `bootstrap` push with `GH_TOKEN`, committing as
`committer` (default `public-sync[bot]`).

## The MCP server

`--target mcp` writes a standalone Model Context Protocol server: one tool per operation marked for MCP, its
`inputSchema` from the operation's parameters and body, an `outputSchema` from its success response, and
`structuredContent` an agent reads as data beside a text rendering. A failure comes back as a tool error with its
status and key, never as a successful result. Read-only operations are annotated as such. It speaks stdio by
default, and Streamable HTTP with `--http`.

```sh
clients generate --spec openapi.json --target mcp --out ./mcp --mcp-name acme
```

Its package publishes to npm as written. `--mcp-package-name @acme/shop-mcp` names it (its bin keeps the server's
name), the metadata block fills its description, license, repository and the rest as it does the TS SDK's, and
`--mcp-mcp-name io.github.acme/shop` writes the `mcpName` the MCP registry checks the npm package by. With it the
server also gets the `server.json` that `mcp-publisher publish` reads from the package's root, on the registry's
2025-12-11 schema: that name, the description (100 characters at most, else refused), the version npm publishes, the
npm package over stdio with every environment variable the server reads, the home page as `websiteUrl`, and a GitHub
or GitLab repository. Where a hosted server runs is yours, so it lists no `remotes`.

```json
{
	"name": "orders_get",
	"inputSchema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "id": { "type": "string" } }, "required": ["id"] },
	"outputSchema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "id": { "type": "string" }, "status": { "type": "string" } } }
}
```

An event stream is one bounded collect: `max_events` (1 to 100, 20 by default) and `last_event_id` in, and
`{ events, last_event_id, ended }` out. When the stream names its events, each event's `event` is required and the
declared names are its `examples`. Each JSON event's `data` is typed by its name in an `anyOf` member, and any other
event, declared or not, has its `data` as a string. A stream of `tick` JSON events and `heartbeat` text events lists
its events as:

```json
{
	"type": "object",
	"properties": { "event": { "type": "string", "examples": ["tick", "heartbeat"] }, "id": { "type": "string" } },
	"required": ["data", "event"],
	"anyOf": [
		{
			"properties": {
				"event": { "const": "tick" },
				"data": { "type": "object", "properties": { "n": { "type": "number" } } }
			}
		},
		{ "properties": { "data": { "type": "string" } } }
	]
}
```

The server reads its configuration from the environment, under the `--mcp-env-prefix` (or the document's title,
upper-cased):

| Variable                     | Default                     | What it does                                                                                      |
| ---------------------------- | --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `$<PREFIX>_BASE_URL`         | the document's first server | the API every call goes to                                                                        |
| `$<PREFIX>_API_KEY`          | none                        | the credential, sent as the document's scheme says; scrubbed from every result                    |
| `$<PREFIX>_HEADERS`          | none                        | a JSON object of headers sent on every call, each scrubbed from results                           |
| `$<PREFIX>_REDIRECT`         | `same-origin`               | `same-origin`, or `follow` to follow a redirect off the API's origin with its credentials dropped |
| `$<PREFIX>_TIMEOUT_MS`       | `30000`                     | each call's bound, an event stream's collect included                                             |
| `$<PREFIX>_FILE_ROOT`        | the client's working dir    | the only directory a `{ path }` file argument is read from                                        |
| `$<PREFIX>_MAX_FILE_BYTES`   | `52428800`                  | the largest file a path may name                                                                  |
| `$<PREFIX>_MAX_INLINE_BYTES` | `1048576`                   | all inline files of one call together, decoded                                                    |
| `$<PREFIX>_MCP_TOKEN`        | none                        | the bearer token `--http` requires; it never reaches the API                                      |

**The standalone server needs Node**: it holds a listening socket and reads local files, so it belongs on a machine
or a container, never on serverless or Workers. To serve the same tools remotely, mount them in the app instead with
`mcp()` from `@workerstack/backend/mcp`, which runs wherever the app runs and is guarded by the app's own auth.

Full reference: [the generated MCP server](https://github.com/workerstack/backend/blob/main/docs/mcp.md).

## Configuring generation

In a backend project the generation is configured once, in the Vite plugin, and `clients generate --app` reads
the same app. `codegen.mcp` writes the handler `mcp()` mounts, and `codegen.openApi` the document the SDKs are
generated from:

```sh
# the whole set, from the app module, in one run
npx clients generate --app src/app.ts \
  --target ts --target go --target python --target cli --target mcp \
  --go-module-path github.com/acme/shop/sdk --cli-repo acme/shop-cli --out generated
```

```json
{
	"scripts": {
		"generate": "backend generate && clients generate --app src/app.ts --target ts --out generated"
	}
}
```

What each target names its package, its client class and its environment variables is the `--<target>-<option>` set
above; nothing is read from a config file of ours, so one command line is the whole input and a CI run cannot drift
from a developer's.

## What a run writes

**Stale files are deleted, edited ones kept.** Each `<out>/<target>` keeps `.clients-generated.json`: every file the
run wrote, with its sha256. A file is rewritten only when its bytes change, through a temp file renamed over it. A
regeneration deletes a file the last run wrote and this one does not (a `cli` target's old `<name>_cmds.go`, say),
unless it was edited since: that one is kept and named on stderr. A file the manifest never listed is never deleted,
nothing outside `<out>/<target>` is touched, and no symlink is followed. Without a manifest, nothing is deleted.

Every target is held to the same conformance grid: one shared scenario suite runs against a live reference server
for all eight targets, and each decoded answer and each request on the wire must match one expected table. A feature
that works in one SDK and breaks in another fails the grid.

To lay the files out yourself, `generated(run, document, ctx)` from `@workerstack/clients` returns each
target's `files` unwritten, each as its text but for the C# package's icon, which is its bytes, and its `packages`:
the package on each registry it publishes to, as `{ registry, name, version }` (`npm` and `jsr` for a scoped TS SDK,
`npm` and `mcp-registry` for an MCP server with an `mcpName`, `pypi`, `crates.io`, `nuget`, `maven-central` as
`group:artifact`, and `go` by the module path, its `/vN` included and no version when none is given).
`writeTarget(dir, files, packages)` writes one target's into a directory you pick under the same rules, keeping
`MANIFEST` (`.clients-generated.json`) there with the packages recorded beside the files, so a release reads each name
and version from it. A file the last call wrote that you leave out of `files` is stale: deleted if unedited, kept and
named in the result's `kept` if you changed it, and dropped from the manifest either way, so a file you take over by
editing is never touched again.

A run kept as data (a release manifest, say) is checked with the same tables the command parses. `TARGETS` lists
every target, and `targetOptionSchemas[target]` is a Standard Schema for that target's options: its option names only,
each a non-empty string, a switch `"true"` or `"false"`. `generated` checks each target's options with it before
anything generates, and `GenerateRun` types them by target, so a misspelled option is a type error, then a refusal.
`GenerateRun`'s `metadata` is the `--metadata-<field>` block as a `Metadata` object, `authors` and `keywords` as
arrays, checked with the same rules.

```ts
import { TARGETS, targetOptionSchemas } from "@workerstack/clients"

const result = targetOptionSchemas.go["~standard"].validate({ modulePath: "github.com/acme/shop-go" })
export const ok = result.issues === undefined && TARGETS.includes("go")
```

This package also exports the app-side generators the backend CLI and Vite plugin use: `generateRouteTree`,
`generateTypes` and `extractTypes` from `@workerstack/clients`, and the command's own entry at
`@workerstack/clients/cli`.

## Releasing a product's public packages

`@workerstack/clients` releases a product's public packages from the private repo that generates them. One
`release.config.ts` lists the packages. `clients release bump` cuts each package's next version from what
changed. `clients release sync` mirrors each package into its own public repo and pushes the `v<version>` tag.
Each public repo's `release.yml` then publishes on that tag through OIDC, with no registry token stored anywhere.
Three reusable workflows in `workerstack/clients` run these steps in CI, so a consumer repo only writes short callers.

### Contents

- [Consumer prerequisites](#consumer-prerequisites)
- [release.config.ts](#releaseconfigts)
- [New product checklist](#new-product-checklist)
- [The reusable workflows](#the-reusable-workflows)
- [CLI](#cli)
- [Versioning](#versioning)
- [Tags](#tags)
- [Deployed spec gate](#deployed-spec-gate)
- [Channels](#channels)
- [Secrets](#secrets)

### Consumer prerequisites

- `@workerstack/clients` in the repo's dependencies. The `workflows-v1` workflows need 1.0.0-rc.25 or later, the first
  version with `release codegen` and `release toolchains`. The workflows run the consumer's own installed copy and pin
  none.
- `@workerstack/system` in the repo's dependencies, and a `system.config.ts` at the repo root that declares every name
  the release config lists in `toolchains`, each at the version codegen needs:

  ```ts
  import { defineConfig } from "@workerstack/system"

  export default defineConfig({ deps: { go: "1.27.2", rust: "1.99.1", uv: "0.13.1", ruff: "0.17.1" } })
  ```

- `packageManager: "bun@<version>"` in the root `package.json` (the workflows read Bun's version from it) and a
  committed `bun.lock` (they run `bun install --frozen-lockfile`, with the repo's scripts on).

### release.config.ts

A product's config sits in its own directory. Each package's source dir is a sibling named after the package, and
every other non-hidden directory there is an error. A package's public repo is `github.com/<repo>`.

```ts
import { defineRelease } from "@workerstack/clients/release"

export default defineRelease({
	project: "<product>",
	/* regenerates every package from the repo root; bump runs it, and it must honor RELEASE_VERSIONS */
	codegen: ["bun", "scripts/codegen.ts"],
	/* the system.config.ts deps codegen needs, installed in this order before it runs */
	toolchains: ["go", "rust", "uv", "ruff"],
	homepage: "https://<domain>",
	metadata: { license: "MIT", authors: ["<Name> <oss@<domain>>"] },
	packages: [
		{
			name: "cli",
			repo: "<org>/cli",
			description: "<one line: the repo's, every registry's, and the first CHANGELOG entry>",
			topics: ["<product>", "cli"],
			commitMessage: "chore: generate from openapi spec",
			clients: {
				target: "cli",
				options: { binaryName: "<bin>", modulePath: "github.com/<org>/cli", repo: "<org>/cli" },
			},
		},
		{
			name: "sdk-typescript",
			repo: "<org>/sdk-typescript",
			description: "<one line>",
			topics: ["<product>", "sdk"],
			commitMessage: "chore: generate from openapi spec",
			clients: { target: "ts" },
			registries: [{ kind: "npm" }, { kind: "jsr" }],
		},
	],
	spec: {
		committedPath: "api/openapi.public.json",
		deployedUrl: "https://api.<domain>/openapi.json",
	},
})
```

| Field                         | Meaning                                                                                                                                         |
| ----------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `project`                     | The product's slug: each package's `<project>/<name>` key, and what codegen filters on                                                          |
| `codegen`                     | The argv that regenerates every package, run from the repo root. Bump runs it again with `RELEASE_VERSIONS` (JSON, package name to version) set |
| `toolchains`                  | Optional, none by default. The `system.config.ts` dep names codegen needs; the workflows install them in this order                             |
| `committer`                   | Optional. The identity sync commits as (`public-sync[bot]` by default); a GitHub App's bot address works                                        |
| `homepage`                    | https. Every public repo's website and every registry's homepage                                                                                |
| `metadata`                    | Optional. Package metadata every generated package carries (authors, license, keywords and the rest); a package's own `metadata` wins over it   |
| `packages[].clients`          | How clients generates the package: its target and that target's options. Absent for a hand-kept package (one that publishes the spec itself)    |
| `packages[].registries`       | Where the public repo's rendered `release.yml` publishes: `npm`, `jsr`, `pypi`, `crates`, `go`, `nuget`, `maven`, or `github` with `assets`     |
| `packages[].branch`           | The public repo's branch sync pushes to, `main` by default                                                                                      |
| `packages[].bootstrapExclude` | Globs the first push leaves out, so the next sync adds them as their own commit                                                                 |
| `spec`                        | The committed spec codegen builds from (repo-relative), and the URL prod serves it at (the deployed spec gate)                                  |

### New product checklist

1. Create or pick the GitHub org for the public repos, and an empty public repo `<org>/<package>` for each package.
   Sync pushes their content; nobody commits there by hand.
2. Register the account-backed channels the packages need. Every registry that supports it publishes through a
   trusted publisher for repo `<org>/<package>`, workflow `release.yml`:
   - JSR: create `@<scope>` and link the package to its repo.
   - npm: npm adds a trusted publisher only to a package that exists, so publish it once by hand with a short-lived
     granular token, add the trusted publisher, then revoke the token.
   - PyPI: add a pending trusted publisher (it works before the first upload).
   - crates.io: publish once with `cargo publish` and a short-lived token, then add the trusted publisher.
   - NuGet: add a trusted-publishing policy for the repo and workflow, and set the repo variable `NUGET_USER` to the
     nuget.org user that owns it.
   - Maven Central has no OIDC: verify the namespace, generate a Portal user token, create a GPG key whose public half
     is on `keys.openpgp.org`, and add the four `MAVEN_*` secrets to the SDK's repo (see [Secrets](#secrets)).
   - Go: nothing to register; the workflow's `proxy.golang.org` fetch indexes the tag.
   - A CLI's channels are clients `cli` options, each optional: a Homebrew tap repo, a Scoop bucket repo, a
     `microsoft/winget-pkgs` fork, an AUR account with an SSH key. Each one's token goes in the CLI's repo.
3. Create a GitHub App with `contents: write`, `workflows: write` (sync pushes each repo's `release.yml`) and
   `administration: write` (sync sets each repo's description, homepage and topics), install it on the org's public repos, and store its ID and private key as two Actions secrets in the private repo.
4. Write `release.config.ts` with a dir per package, add the prerequisites above, and check the config:
   `clients release sync --config <path> --validate-only`. A CLI also needs a hand `README.md` and `LICENSE`;
   clients writes its `.goreleaser.yaml` and `.github/workflows/release.yml`.
5. Publishing needs no workflow edits: every public tree carries a `release.yml` (the CLI's from clients, the rest
   rendered from `registries`). Before the first real tag, run a repo's `release.yml` by hand with `workflow_dispatch`
   to see each registry accept it. A repo whose version is already live must get that tag pushed by hand before its
   first `release.yml` lands, or sync tags and republishes it.
6. First release: commit the spec (bump records the commit a release is cut from), run the bump caller (or
   `clients release bump --config <path>` locally), and merge the release PR. Each package releases 1.0.0 with
   its `description` as the entry. The next sync tags each package.
7. Verify: each public repo's `release` run is green (`gh run list -R <org>/<package> -w release`), its GitHub release
   has its assets, each registry serves the new version, and a CLI's tap, bucket, winget PR and AUR package show it.

### The reusable workflows

A consumer calls each one from its own workflow, pinned to the `workflows-v1` tag. The caller owns the triggers,
the `concurrency` group and the permissions it grants. A reusable workflow's job never gets more than its caller
grants, and secrets pass only through the declared `secrets:`, never `secrets: inherit` across owners. Every job runs
the same set-up: checkout, Node 24 (the release config loads as TypeScript), Bun from `packageManager`,
`bun install --frozen-lockfile`, each `toolchains` name through `system install <name> --upgrade` at its
`system.config.ts` pin with those tools first on PATH, then `release codegen`.

Each workflow also takes `cli`, the command that runs clients, split on spaces. It defaults to
`bun x --no-install clients`, the bin a consumer's `@workerstack/clients` install links. A consumer leaves it
unset. This repo's own release fixture passes `node bin/clients.js`, because bun never links a root package's
own bin.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/release-sync.yml
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths: ["<product>-release/**", "api/**"]
  schedule: [{ cron: "0 3 * * *" }]
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      dry-run: { type: boolean, default: false }
      only: { type: string, required: false }
concurrency: { group: release-sync, cancel-in-progress: false }
permissions: { contents: read }
jobs:
  sync:
    uses: workerstack/clients/.github/workflows/release-sync.yml@workflows-v1
    with:
      config: <product>-release/release.config.ts
      app-owner: <org>
      dry-run: ${{ inputs.dry-run == true }}
      only: ${{ inputs.only }}
    secrets:
      app-id: ${{ secrets.RELEASE_APP_ID }}
      app-private-key: ${{ secrets.RELEASE_APP_PRIVATE_KEY }}
```

| `release-sync.yml`          | Meaning                                                                                                                    |
| --------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `config`                    | Required. The release config, repo-relative                                                                                |
| `app-owner`                 | The App installation's owner (the public repos' org); blank means the caller repo's owner                                  |
| `dry-run`                   | Stage each tree and report what would be pushed and tagged, pushing nothing                                                |
| `only`                      | Comma-separated package names (`name` or `project/name`); blank means every package                                        |
| `app-id`, `app-private-key` | Secrets, optional. Without both, the token step is skipped and only a dry run works (sync says `GH_TOKEN env is required`) |

```yaml
# .github/workflows/release-bump.yml
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      major: { type: boolean, default: false }
permissions: { contents: write, pull-requests: write }
jobs:
  bump:
    uses: workerstack/clients/.github/workflows/release-bump.yml@workflows-v1
    with:
      config: <product>-release/release.config.ts
      major: ${{ inputs.major == true }}
```

`release-bump.yml` takes `config` (required) and `major` (release every changed package as a major). It also installs
`go` when `toolchains` does not list it, because bump runs oasdiff through `go run`. When a package changed, it opens
or updates the release PR on branch `auto/release-bump` with exactly the paths bump printed as `wrote:`. That PR is
opened with the caller's `GITHUB_TOKEN`, so it starts no workflows of its own: run the validate caller by hand, or
review the PR's diff.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/release-validate.yml
on:
  pull_request:
    paths: ["<product>-release/**"]
permissions: { contents: read }
jobs:
  validate:
    uses: workerstack/clients/.github/workflows/release-validate.yml@workflows-v1
    with:
      config: <product>-release/release.config.ts
```

`release-validate.yml` takes `config` and runs the set-up, codegen, then `release sync --validate-only`.

A dry run proves the whole path short of the push: the toolchains install, codegen runs, every package's tree is
staged against its public repo's current tip, its `release.yml` is rendered, and the report says which packages would
be pushed and which `v<version>` tags would be created. It leaves out the push, the tag and the repo settings step.

### CLI

```
clients release bump --config <path> [--major]
clients release sync --config <path> [--only <names>] [--dry-run] [--validate-only]
clients release bootstrap --config <path> (--all | --only <names>) [--force-bootstrap]
clients release codegen --config <path>
clients release toolchains --config <path>
```

- `bump` regenerates, decides each package's release, gates generated output on prod, writes versions, regenerates at
  them, and records the release. It prints one `bumped: <name> <version> <kind>` line per release and one
  `wrote: <path>` line per file it touched.
- `sync` mirrors each package and pushes its tag. It needs `GH_TOKEN` unless `--dry-run` or `--validate-only` is set.
- `bootstrap` makes the first push to an empty public repo, or over the stub a new repo starts with.
- `codegen` runs the config's codegen from the repo root, as bump runs it.
- `toolchains` prints the config's `toolchains`, one per line.

### Versioning

`bump` runs the product's codegen, then compares each package with what its `.release-state.json` recorded at the last
release. It compares the generated output (backend's `.clients-generated.json` map, or the spec itself for a hand-kept
package) and the tracked hand files (version lines normalized, the CHANGELOG and the state file left out). Nothing
moved means no release, even when the spec moved.

When the output changed on a moved spec, oasdiff compares the spec with the one the last release was cut from (read
back with `git show <commit>:<path>`). Any API change, breaking or not, is a minor. Output that changed with no API change,
and any hand-file change, is a patch. A package stays on its major line: a major comes only from `--major`, which makes each
package that releases a major.

A release writes the new version into every version file the package has (`package.json`, `jsr.json`,
`pyproject.toml`). It reruns codegen with `RELEASE_VERSIONS`, so version-baked output is regenerated at that version.
Only then does it record the digests, the spec's commit and the version in `.release-state.json`, so the merged release
PR finds nothing left to release. The spec must be committed first, because the state records HEAD. A refusal writes
nothing, so a rerun decides the same. Each public repo's `release.yml` checks the tag against its version files, so a
tag whose files disagree fails before anything publishes.

### Tags

Sync tags; the private repo never does. After sync pushes a package, or finds the bot's tip already equal to the
source, it pushes `v<version>` from the package's `.release-state.json` unless that tag exists. It never moves a tag,
so a rerun, or a run after one that stopped between its commit and its tag, converges. A merged release PR therefore
releases every bumped package on the next sync. Never delete or move a pushed tag.

### Deployed spec gate

Generated code may only describe operations prod serves. The gate fetches `spec.deployedUrl` and compares it with the
committed spec by canonical sha. Sync refuses a package whose changed paths include a file clients generated. Bump
refuses the whole run, hand-kept packages included, when a generated package whose output changed would release. On
drift both print both shas and the operations on either side. Deploy, then rerun the bump caller; sync reruns on its
schedule.

### Channels

| Package kind               | Channel                                                                                       | Published by                              |
| -------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| CLI                        | GitHub Release: archives, `checksums.txt` signed by cosign, build attestations, `version.txt` | backend's `release.yml` in the CLI's repo |
| CLI                        | Homebrew cask, Scoop manifest, winget PR, AUR `<bin>-bin`, deb/rpm/apk assets (each optional) | the same, with its channel's secret       |
| TypeScript SDK, MCP server | npm (provenance), JSR                                                                         | the rendered `release.yml`                |
| Go SDK                     | the Go proxy (`proxy.golang.org` fetch of the tag)                                            | the rendered `release.yml`                |
| Python SDK                 | PyPI (attestations)                                                                           | the rendered `release.yml`                |
| Rust SDK                   | crates.io                                                                                     | the rendered `release.yml`                |
| C# SDK                     | NuGet                                                                                         | the rendered `release.yml`                |
| Java SDK                   | Maven Central (GPG-signed bundle through the Central Portal)                                  | the rendered `release.yml`                |
| OpenAPI spec               | GitHub Release with `openapi.json`                                                            | the rendered `release.yml`                |

A rendered `release.yml` checks the tag against the version each registry publishes from, publishes, and retries until
the registry serves the version. A rejected or repeated upload fails the run; a rerun is `workflow_dispatch` with the
tag. Go modules at 2.0.0 and up carry `/v<major>` in their path, which codegen adds for the go and cli targets.

### Secrets

| Secret                                             | Where            | Read by                                                                           |
| -------------------------------------------------- | ---------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| the App's ID and private key                       | the private repo | the sync caller, passed as `app-id` and `app-private-key`                         |
| `HOMEBREW_TAP_TOKEN`                               | `<org>/cli`      | goreleaser's cask push to the tap                                                 |
| `SCOOP_BUCKET_TOKEN`                               | `<org>/cli`      | goreleaser's manifest push to the bucket                                          |
| `WINGET_TOKEN`                                     | `<org>/cli`      | goreleaser's push to the winget-pkgs fork and its PR to `microsoft/winget-pkgs`   |
| `AUR_SSH_KEY`                                      | `<org>/cli`      | goreleaser's push to `aur.archlinux.org/<bin>-bin.git`                            |
| none for npm, JSR, PyPI, crates.io, NuGet          |                  | trusted publishers; NuGet's login also reads the repo variable `NUGET_USER`       |
| `MAVEN_CENTRAL_USERNAME`, `MAVEN_CENTRAL_PASSWORD` | `<org>/sdk-java` | the Central Portal user token: uploads the bundle and polls until it is published |
| `MAVEN_GPG_PRIVATE_KEY`, `MAVEN_GPG_PASSPHRASE`    | `<org>/sdk-java` | signs every bundle file; the public key must be on a keyserver Central reads      |

## Gates

### Script contract

This repo has these `package.json` scripts. Hooks and CI call only these names, so a tool change is one line in `package.json`.

| script                       | runs                                                                                      |
| ---------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `fmt` / `fmt:check`          | `repo fmt`: oxfmt with the standards pack's generated `.oxfmtrc.jsonc`                    |
| `lint` / `lint:fix`          | `repo lint`: oxlint with the generated `.oxlintrc.jsonc`, the repo's own plugin in `lint/` |
| `typecheck`                  | `tsc -p tsconfig.json`: src, tests and scripts                                            |
| `typecheck:src`              | `tsc -p tsconfig.src.json`: the source under the strict preset                            |
| `test`                       | the repo's suite                                                                          |

The lint and format configs, `knip.jsonc` and the git hooks are written by `bun repo sync` from `repo.config.ts`. The
repo's own lint rules are `lint.plugins` and `lint.rules` there; a rule that does not fit a file is a `lint.skip` entry
with its reason, and a use knip cannot see is a `knip.ignore` entry with its reason.

### Where each gate runs

| when       | what                                                                                                                         | blocks                |
| ---------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------- |
| pre-commit | `repo precommit`: fmt and `lint --fix` on the staged files (restaged), lint held to the baseline, typecheck, sync, the related tests, `repo check` | the commit            |
| commit-msg | `repo commit-msg`: Conventional Commits and the change-size rule                                                             | the commit            |
| pre-push   | `repo link --pre-push`, then `repo commit-msg --pre-push` on each pushed commit                                              | the push              |
| CI         | on every push to `main`: the `commits` job (`repo commit-msg --range`), `fmt:check`, `repo check`, `typecheck`, `typecheck:src`, `test`, `test:harness` | new work, until fixed |

`bun repo sync` points `core.hooksPath` at `.githooks/`, so the hooks come with `bun install`.

### Push and CI

No full suite runs locally. Each commit runs the tests its change reaches: the touched test files and the tests of the code it changed. Then push, and run `bun repo ci wait` in the background. It waits for CI's run on the pushed commit and names any failed job and its log. A push cancels the run before it, so batch the commits and push once.

### Release

The version bump rides in the final push. Only a commit CI passed on `main` gets the `v*` tag. The release workflow runs no tests: it waits for that commit's `ci.yml` push run and publishes on its success, so a bump made after the green push is a new commit and costs another CI run. The tag's notes are the `## [Unreleased]` entry of `CHANGELOG.md` for a prerelease and the dated `## [x.y.z] - YYYY-MM-DD` entry for a final release; `scripts/changelog.ts` refuses a tag without them.

### Browsers

- Chrome: `offscreen --hypr` adds a hidden virtual monitor to the running Hyprland; tests drive Chrome on it over CDP. It never takes focus. `exec` and `run` are refused in that mode.
- Safari: the MacBook Air M3 over Tailscale (`ssh mac`, `safaridriver -p 4799`), one run at a time.

## Red, fix, green

1. Red: write the test that shows the bug or the missing behavior. Run it. It must fail, for the reason the test names. Record the failing output (BUGS.md for a bug, where the repo has one).
2. Fix: the smallest change that makes it pass.
3. Green: run it again and record the passing output. Then run the tests the change reaches, and leave the full gates to CI on the push.

A test that cannot fail proves nothing. Check it: revert or break the fix, and the test must go red.

Commits: the test and the fix may share a commit or come as `test(...)` then `fix(...)`. A `fix` or `feat` commit always contains a test change.

Lint rules follow the same loop. A mistake that a rule could catch mechanically ships with a rule: a RuleTester case that fails first, then the rule, in the repo's `lint/` plugin.
